Asymptotically attaining the Moore bound

W. Cames van Batenburg Note: Département d’Informatique, Université libre de Bruxelles, Belgium (w.p.s.camesvanbatenburg@gmail.com). Supported by the Belgian National Fund for Scientific Research (FNRS).    S. Korsky Note: Independent researcher, (samkorsky11@gmail.com).
August 24, 2026
Abstract

For positive integers dd and kk, let nk​(d)n_{k}(d) be the maximum order of a graph of maximum degree at most dd and diameter at most kk. We prove that

limd→∞nk​(d)dk=1\lim_{d\to\infty}\frac{n_{k}(d)}{d^{k}}=1

for every fixed kk, thereby resolving the asymptotic degree–diameter problem for fixed diameter and proving a conjecture of Bollobás. The lower bound comes from regular graphs Hk,qH_{k,q}, indexed by prime powers qq, whose vertices are partial flags in 𝔽q 2​k+1\mathbb{F}_{q}^{\,2k+1}. These graphs have diameter kk and order |V⁡(Hk,q)|=(1+o⁡(1))​Δ​(Hk,q)k|V(H_{k,q})|=(1+o(1))\Delta(H_{k,q})^{k}. We also construct, for every fixed ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2, graphs of maximum degree at most dd and line-graph diameter at most ℓ\ell with (1+o⁡(1))​dℓ(1+o(1))d^{\ell} edges.

1 Introduction

Let kk and dd be positive integers. At most how many vertices can a graph GG have if its maximum degree Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G) is at most dd and its diameter diam⁡G\diam G is at most kk? In this work we obtain an asymptotically tight answer to that question. Define

nk​(d):=max⁡{|V⁡(G)|:Δ⁡(G)≤d​ and ​diam⁡G≤k}.n_{k}(d):=\max\{|V(G)|:\Delta(G)\leq d\text{ and }\diam G\leq k\}. (1)

A breadth-first search from any vertex gives the Moore bound

nk​(d)≤1+d​∑j=0k−1(d−1)j=dk+Ok​(dk−1).n_{k}(d)\leq 1+d\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(d-1)^{j}=d^{k}+O_{k}(d^{k-1}). (2)

A graph attaining equality in the Moore bound is called a Moore graph. Complete graphs attain the bound when k=1k=1, and the odd cycle C2​k+1C_{2k+1} attains it when d=2d=2. Apart from these families and the trivial degree-one cases, the Petersen graph and the Hoffman–Singleton graph attain the bound for (d,k)=(3,2)(d,k)=(3,2) and (7,2)(7,2), respectively. The only remaining potential nontrivial Moore graph would have degree 5757 and diameter 22; no Moore graph exists for any other parameters [19, 4, 14]. We refer to the survey of Miller and Širáň [21] for further background on the degree–diameter problem.

The rarity of exact equality leads naturally to the asymptotic problem in which kk is fixed and dd tends to infinity. Bollobás conjectured that, for every fixed k≥2k\geq 2 and every ε>0\varepsilon>0, there are infinitely many dd for which

nk​(d)≥(1−ε)​dk;n_{k}(d)\geq(1-\varepsilon)d^{k};

equivalently, lim supd→∞nk​(d)dk=1\limsup_{d\to\infty}\frac{n_{k}(d)}{d^{k}}=1; see the discussion in [8, p. 2]. This longstanding conjecture was previously known only for k∈{2,3,5}k\in\{2,3,5\}, through constructions arising from finite generalized polygons [16, 17, 3]. For all sufficiently large kk, Canale and Gómez proved that infinitely many degrees Δ\Delta admit a graph of diameter kk and order greater than (0.629​Δ)k(0.629\,\Delta)^{k} [11]; see also [8, Proposition 5]. This was the strongest coefficient known uniformly over all sufficiently large diameters. Another variant of Bollobás’ conjecture [6, 7] is that lim infd→∞nk​(d)dk=1\liminf_{d\to\infty}\frac{n_{k}(d)}{d^{k}}=1. We prove that stronger statement.

Theorem 1.1.

For every fixed positive integer kk,

limd→∞nk​(d)dk=1.\lim_{d\to\infty}\frac{n_{k}(d)}{d^{k}}=1. (3)

Our construction uses complete flags in 𝔽q2​k+1\mathbb{F}_{q}^{2k+1}. The vertices are the even-rank subflags, and two vertices are adjacent when some odd-rank subflag extends both to complete flags. Any two complete flags are induced by two orderings of a common basis. Odd-even transposition sorting (alternating rounds of disjoint adjacent swaps) transforms one ordering into the other, and since only every second round changes the even ranks, the corresponding vertices are joined by a path of length at most kk. Each vertex has exactly (q+1)k(q+1)^{k} extensions to a complete flag, yielding a natural upper bound on the degree of the graph. The Moore bound shows that this upper bound is asymptotically tight, and the prime number theorem supplies suitable field sizes for all sufficiently large degree bounds.

We also consider the edge version of the problem, posed by Erdős and Nešetřil [18] and studied recently by Cambie, Cames van Batenburg, de Joannis de Verclos, and Kang [8]. For positive integers ℓ\ell and dd, write

hℓ​(d)−1:=max⁡{|E⁡(G)|:Δ⁡(G)≤d​ and ​diam⁡L⁡(G)≤ℓ},h_{\ell}(d)-1:=\max\{|E(G)|:\Delta(G)\leq d\text{ and }\diam L(G)\leq\ell\}, (4)

where L⁡(G)L(G) is the line graph of GG. Cambie et al. conjectured that, for every fixed ℓ\ell and every ε>0\varepsilon>0, hℓ​(d)≥(1−ε)​dℓh_{\ell}(d)\geq(1-\varepsilon)d^{\ell} for infinitely many dd [8, Conjecture 3]. We prove the stronger liminf statement.

Corollary 1.2.

For every fixed integer ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2,

lim infd→∞hℓ​(d)dℓ≥1.\liminf_{d\to\infty}\frac{h_{\ell}(d)}{d^{\ell}}\geq 1. (5)

The graphs used to prove Corollary 1.2 are bipartite. Together with the matching upper bound for odd-cycle-free graphs in [8, Theorem 7], this also shows that the limit is 11 when restricted to bipartite graphs. In contrast, for general graphs the bound is not tight. For ℓ=2\ell=2, it is known [12] that h2​(d)d2\frac{h_{2}(d)}{d^{2}} converges to 54\frac{5}{4}, which is attained by blown-up 55-cycles and is related to the infamous Erdős–Nešetřil conjecture on coloring the square of a line graph; see [13, 9, 15] for more background. For ℓ=3\ell=3, Kumar, Mohar and Pragada [20] recently showed that lim infd→∞h3​(d)d3≥253225\liminf_{d\to\infty}\frac{h_{3}(d)}{d^{3}}\geq\frac{253}{225} is strictly larger than 11. For ℓ∈{4,6}\ell\in\{4,6\}, the lower bound 11 was known to follow from geometric constructions similar to those used for the vertex version. For all sufficiently large values of ℓ\ell, our Corollary 1.2 improves the lower bound from (0.629)ℓ(0.629)^{\ell} to 11. For all ℓ≥3\ell\geq 3, the current best upper bound [8] is 3/23/2.

2 Alternating routes between complete flags

Let VV be a tt-dimensional vector space. A complete flag in VV is an increasing chain of subspaces

F=(0=F0<F1<⋯<Ft−1<Ft=V),dimFi=i.F=(0=F_{0}<F_{1}<\cdots<F_{t-1}<F_{t}=V),\qquad\dim F_{i}=i.

Write

Fodd:=(Fi)1≤i<ti​ odd,Feven:=(Fi)1≤i<ti​ even.F_{\mathrm{odd}}:=(F_{i})_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq i<t\\ i\text{ odd}\end{subarray}},\qquad F_{\mathrm{even}}:=(F_{i})_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq i<t\\ i\text{ even}\end{subarray}}.
Lemma 2.1.

Let FF and F′F^{\prime} be complete flags in a tt-dimensional vector space. There is a sequence of complete flags

F=G0,G1,…,Gt=F′F=G^{0},G^{1},\ldots,G^{t}=F^{\prime}

such that, at odd-numbered steps, only odd-rank members may change, and at even-numbered steps, only even-rank members may change.

By the standard fact that any two complete flags are induced by two orderings of a common basis (see the proof of axiom (B1) in [1, Section 4.3, pp. 183–184]), there are a basis v1,…,vtv_{1},\ldots,v_{t} and a permutation π∈St\pi\in S_{t} such that

Fi=span(v1,…,vi),Fi′=span(vπ⁡(1),…,vπ⁡(i))(0≤i≤t).F_{i}=\operatorname{span}(v_{1},\ldots,v_{i}),\qquad F^{\prime}_{i}=\operatorname{span}(v_{\pi(1)},\ldots,v_{\pi(i)})\quad(0\leq i\leq t).

Label viv_{i} by its target position π−1​(i)\pi^{-1}(i) and apply odd–even transposition sorting to these labels. This transforms the order v1,…,vtv_{1},\ldots,v_{t} into vπ⁡(1),…,vπ⁡(t)v_{\pi(1)},\ldots,v_{\pi(t)}. Allowing stationary steps, it uses tt alternating rounds [2, p. 518]. In an odd round one swaps a subset of the disjoint adjacent pairs

(1,2),(3,4),…,(1,2),(3,4),\ldots,

and in an even round one swaps a subset of

(2,3),(4,5),….(2,3),(4,5),\ldots.

Swapping the vectors in positions ii and i+1i+1 changes only the ii-dimensional prefix span. An odd round therefore changes only odd-rank members of the associated flag, and an even round changes only even-rank members. The associated flags give the required route. ∎

For a tt-dimensional vector space VV, let ℱ⁡(V)\mathcal{F}(V) be its set of complete flags, and set

𝒫odd​(V):={Fodd:F∈ℱ⁡(V)},𝒫even​(V):={Feven:F∈ℱ⁡(V)}.\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{odd}}(V):=\{F_{\mathrm{odd}}:F\in\mathcal{F}(V)\},\qquad\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{even}}(V):=\{F_{\mathrm{even}}:F\in\mathcal{F}(V)\}.

An odd-rank partial flag FoddF_{\mathrm{odd}} and an even-rank partial flag FevenF_{\mathrm{even}} are called compatible if their members, interleaved by rank, form a complete flag. A compatible pair determines that complete flag uniquely.

For a prime power qq, write

[j]q:=1+q+⋯+qj−1,[t]q!:=∏j=1t[j]q.[j]_{q}:=1+q+\cdots+q^{j-1},\qquad[t]_{q}!:=\prod_{j=1}^{t}[j]_{q}.

Thus [t]q![t]_{q}! is the number of complete flags in 𝔽qt\mathbb{F}_{q}^{t}.

3 The halved flag construction

Fix k≥1k\geq 1, let t=2​k+1t=2k+1, and take V=𝔽qtV=\mathbb{F}_{q}^{t}. Define Hk,qH_{k,q} to be the graph with vertex set 𝒫even​(V)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{even}}(V) in which two distinct vertices are adjacent if they have a common compatible member of 𝒫odd​(V)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{odd}}(V). Equivalently, Hk,qH_{k,q} is obtained by taking the square of the bipartite compatibility graph between 𝒫even​(V)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{even}}(V) and 𝒫odd​(V)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{odd}}(V), and then restricting to the vertices that represent 𝒫even​(V)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{even}}(V). Via the last step we only retain half the vertices, so in this sense we have “halved the flags.”

Proposition 3.1.

For every prime power qq and every k≥1k\geq 1, the graph Hk,qH_{k,q} is regular. Writing Δq\Delta_{q} for its degree, we have

Nq:=|V⁡(Hk,q)|=[2​k+1]q!(q+1)k,N_{q}:=|V(H_{k,q})|=\frac{[2k+1]_{q}!}{(q+1)^{k}}, (6)
Δq≤Kq:=(q+1)k​((q+1)k−1),\Delta_{q}\leq K_{q}:=(q+1)^{k}\left((q+1)^{k}-1\right), (7)

and

diam⁡Hk,q=k.\diam H_{k,q}=k. (8)

For fixed kk, as q→∞q\to\infty through prime powers,

Δq=(1+o⁡(1))​Kq,Nq=(1+o⁡(1))​Δqk.\Delta_{q}=(1+o(1))K_{q},\qquad N_{q}=(1+o(1))\Delta_{q}^{k}. (9)

Order and degree. There are kk odd and kk even ranks among 1,…,t−11,\ldots,t-1. Fix Peven∈𝒫even​(V)P_{\mathrm{even}}\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{even}}(V). For each odd i∈{1,…,t−1}i\in\{1,\ldots,t-1\}, a completion to a full flag must choose an intermediate space

(Peven)i−1<Fi<(Peven)i+1,(P_{\mathrm{even}})_{i-1}<F_{i}<(P_{\mathrm{even}})_{i+1},

where F0=0F_{0}=0 and Ft=VF_{t}=V are understood. The corresponding quotient has dimension two, and hence there are q+1q+1 choices for FiF_{i}. These choices are independent, so every even-rank partial flag has exactly (q+1)k(q+1)^{k} completions. The same argument applies to odd-rank partial flags. Counting complete flags by their even-rank parts proves (6).

Any two even-rank partial flags are carried to one another by an invertible linear map. Since invertible linear maps preserve compatibility, they induce automorphisms of Hk,qH_{k,q}. Thus Hk,qH_{k,q} is vertex-transitive and hence regular. From a fixed vertex there are exactly (q+1)k(q+1)^{k} compatible odd-rank partial flags, and each of these is compatible with exactly (q+1)k−1(q+1)^{k}-1 other even-rank partial flags. Different odd-rank partial flags may yield the same neighbor, so (7) follows.

Diameter. Take Peven,Peven′∈𝒫even​(V)P_{\mathrm{even}},P^{\prime}_{\mathrm{even}}\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{even}}(V) and complete them to full flags FF and F′F^{\prime}. Apply Lemma 2.1 to obtain an odd-first route

F=G0,G1,…,Gt=F′.F=G^{0},G^{1},\ldots,G^{t}=F^{\prime}.

For 0≤j≤k0\leq j\leq k, set

Pj:=(G2​j)even=(G2​j+1)even,P_{j}:=(G^{2j})_{\mathrm{even}}=(G^{2j+1})_{\mathrm{even}},

and, for 1≤j≤k1\leq j\leq k, set

Qj:=(G2​j−1)odd=(G2​j)odd.Q_{j}:=(G^{2j-1})_{\mathrm{odd}}=(G^{2j})_{\mathrm{odd}}.

The equality for PjP_{j} holds because odd steps leave all even-rank members unchanged, while the equality for QjQ_{j} holds because even steps leave all odd-rank members unchanged. Thus QjQ_{j} is compatible with Pj−1P_{j-1} via G2​j−1G^{2j-1} and with PjP_{j} via G2​jG^{2j}. Hence

Pj−1​ and ​Pj​ are either equal or adjacent in ​Hk,q.P_{j-1}\text{ and }P_{j}\text{ are either equal or adjacent in }H_{k,q}.

Finally, since G0=FG^{0}=F and Gt=F′G^{t}=F^{\prime}, we have P0=PevenP_{0}=P_{\mathrm{even}} and Pk=Peven′P_{k}=P^{\prime}_{\mathrm{even}}. Deleting repetitions gives a path of length at most kk.

For the reverse inequality, fix a basis e1,…,ete_{1},\ldots,e_{t}. For an odd- or even-rank partial flag R=(Ri)R=(R_{i}), put

λ⁡(R):=max⁡({i:e1∉Ri}∪{0}).\lambda(R):=\max\left(\{i:e_{1}\notin R_{i}\}\cup\{0\}\right).

Thus λ⁡(R)\lambda(R) is the last recorded rank before e1e_{1} appears. If R∈𝒫even​(V)R\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{even}}(V) and S∈𝒫odd​(V)S\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{odd}}(V) are compatible, let rr be the first rank at which e1e_{1} occurs in their common complete flag. Then λ⁡(R)\lambda(R) and λ⁡(S)\lambda(S) are the largest even and odd ranks below rr, respectively, so

|λ⁡(R)−λ⁡(S)|≤1.|\lambda(R)-\lambda(S)|\leq 1.

It follows that adjacent vertices of Hk,qH_{k,q} have λ\lambda-values differing by at most two. For the standard and opposite complete flags

Ai=span⁡(e1,…,ei),Ci=span⁡(et,et−1,…,et+1−i),A_{i}=\operatorname{span}(e_{1},\ldots,e_{i}),\qquad C_{i}=\operatorname{span}(e_{t},e_{t-1},\ldots,e_{t+1-i}),

one has

λ⁡(Aeven)=0,λ⁡(Ceven)=2​k.\lambda(A_{\mathrm{even}})=0,\qquad\lambda(C_{\mathrm{even}})=2k.

A path of length ss between these vertices would therefore satisfy 2​k≤2​s2k\leq 2s, so s≥ks\geq k. This proves (8).

Asymptotics. For fixed kk, we have [2​k+1]q!=qk⁡(2​k+1)​(1+Ok​(q−1)).[2k+1]_{q}!=q^{k(2k+1)}\left(1+O_{k}(q^{-1})\right). Equations (6) and (7) give Nq=q2​k2​(1+Ok​(q−1))N_{q}=q^{2k^{2}}\left(1+O_{k}(q^{-1})\right) and Kq=q2​k​(1+Ok​(q−1))K_{q}=q^{2k}\left(1+O_{k}(q^{-1})\right), and hence

Nq=(1+Ok​(q−1))​Kqk.N_{q}=\left(1+O_{k}(q^{-1})\right)K_{q}^{k}. (10)

Since Nq→∞N_{q}\to\infty, the Moore bound forces Δq→∞\Delta_{q}\to\infty, and hence Nq≤(1+o⁡(1))​ΔqkN_{q}\leq(1+o(1))\Delta_{q}^{k}. Together with (10) and Δq≤Kq\Delta_{q}\leq K_{q}, this gives Δq∼Kq\Delta_{q}\sim K_{q}, and therefore Nq∼ΔqkN_{q}\sim\Delta_{q}^{k}. This proves (9). ∎

The case k=1k=1 follows from the complete graph Kd+1K_{d+1}. Fix k≥2k\geq 2 and let d→∞d\to\infty. Let qq be the largest prime not exceeding d1/(2​k)−1d^{1/(2k)}-1. The prime number theorem gives q=(1+o⁡(1))​d1/(2​k)q=(1+o(1))d^{1/(2k)}. For this choice,

Δ⁡(Hk,q)≤Kq<(q+1)2​k≤d,Kq=(1+o⁡(1))​d.\Delta(H_{k,q})\leq K_{q}<(q+1)^{2k}\leq d,\qquad K_{q}=(1+o(1))d.

Proposition 3.1 therefore yields

nk​(d)≥Nq=(1+o⁡(1))​Kqk=(1+o⁡(1))​dk.n_{k}(d)\geq N_{q}=(1+o(1))K_{q}^{k}=(1+o(1))d^{k}.

Together with the Moore bound (2), this proves (3). ∎

Remark 3.2.

For fixed k≥2k\geq 2, the explicit degree bound in Proposition 3.1 gives

|V⁡(Hk,q)|1/kΔ⁡(Hk,q)≥Nq1/kKq=1−2​k−1q+Ok​(q−2).\frac{|V(H_{k,q})|^{1/k}}{\Delta(H_{k,q})}\geq\frac{N_{q}^{1/k}}{K_{q}}=1-\frac{2k-1}{q}+O_{k}(q^{-2}).

More involved variants can improve the coefficient of q−1q^{-1}, but we have chosen the halved construction because it gives the shortest and most transparent proof. It would be interesting to determine, for fixed kk, the optimal rate at which nk​(d)/dkn_{k}(d)/d^{k} tends to one. This is particularly relevant in light of the following two questions asked by Bermond and Bollobás [5], which remain open. Let Mk​(d)=1+d​∑j=0k−1(d−1)jM_{k}(d)=1+d\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(d-1)^{j} denote the Moore bound. Does nk​(d)Mk​(d)\frac{n_{k}(d)}{M_{k}(d)} converge to 11 along every sequence of pairs (k,d)(k,d) for which both kk and dd tend to infinity, and is Mk​(d)−nk​(d)M_{k}(d)-n_{k}(d) unbounded?

4 The edge version

Given a graph HH, define a bipartite graph B⁡(H)B(H) with parts V​(H)0V(H)_{0} and V​(H)1V(H)_{1} by joining x0x_{0} to y1y_{1} whenever x=yx=y or x​y∈E⁡(H)xy\in E(H).

Lemma 4.1.

For every graph HH,

diam⁡L⁡(B⁡(H))≤diam⁡H+1.\diam L(B(H))\leq\diam H+1.

Let diam⁡H≤k\diam H\leq k, and write an edge x0​y1x_{0}y_{1} of B⁡(H)B(H) as [x,y][x,y]. Take two edges e=[a,b]e=[a,b] and f=[c,d]f=[c,d]. If kk is odd, choose a sequence

b=z0,z1,…,zr=cb=z_{0},z_{1},\ldots,z_{r}=c

of odd length r≤kr\leq k in which consecutive terms are equal or adjacent in HH. If kk is even, choose such a sequence from bb to dd of even length r≤kr\leq k. Such a sequence exists by taking a shortest path and, if necessary, repeating one vertex once.

Starting from [a,z0][a,z_{0}], alternately replace the first and second coordinates:

[a,z0],[z1,z0],[z1,z2],[z3,z2],….[a,z_{0}],[z_{1},z_{0}],[z_{1},z_{2}],[z_{3},z_{2}],\ldots.

Every displayed pair is an edge of B⁡(H)B(H), and consecutive pairs share an endpoint. After rr replacements, the last edge shares its 00-side endpoint with ff when rr is odd, and its 11-side endpoint with ff when rr is even. Thus ee and ff are at distance at most r+1≤k+1r+1\leq k+1 in L⁡(B⁡(H))L(B(H)). ∎

Fix ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2, put k=ℓ−1k=\ell-1, and let d→∞d\to\infty. Let qq be the largest prime not exceeding d1/(2​k)−1d^{1/(2k)}-1, and put H=Hk,qH=H_{k,q}. Write Nq=|V⁡(H)|N_{q}=|V(H)| and Δq=Δ⁡(H)\Delta_{q}=\Delta(H), and form G=B⁡(H)G=B(H). Since HH is Δq\Delta_{q}-regular, GG is (Δq+1)(\Delta_{q}+1)-regular and

|E⁡(G)|=Nq​(Δq+1).|E(G)|=N_{q}(\Delta_{q}+1).

Moreover,

Δ⁡(G)=Δq+1≤Kq+1<(q+1)2​k≤d,\Delta(G)=\Delta_{q}+1\leq K_{q}+1<(q+1)^{2k}\leq d,

and Lemma 4.1 gives

diam⁡L⁡(G)≤k+1=ℓ.\diam L(G)\leq k+1=\ell.

The prime number theorem and Proposition 3.1 give

Kq=(1+o⁡(1))​d,Δq=(1+o⁡(1))​d,Nq=(1+o⁡(1))​Δqk.K_{q}=(1+o(1))d,\qquad\Delta_{q}=(1+o(1))d,\qquad N_{q}=(1+o(1))\Delta_{q}^{k}.

Consequently,

|E⁡(G)|=Nq​(Δq+1)=(1+o⁡(1))​dk+1=(1+o⁡(1))​dℓ.|E(G)|=N_{q}(\Delta_{q}+1)=(1+o(1))d^{k+1}=(1+o(1))d^{\ell}.

Since hℓ​(d)−1≥|E⁡(G)|h_{\ell}(d)-1\geq|E(G)|, this proves (5).

The graph GG is bipartite. Conversely, Theorem 7 (or more precisely, Theorem 10) of [8] implies that every bipartite graph of maximum degree at most dd and line-graph diameter at most ℓ\ell has at most dℓd^{\ell} edges. Thus the maximum number of edges in the bipartite version is (1+o⁡(1))​dℓ(1+o(1))d^{\ell}. ∎

After this work was completed, we learned that the projective-plane construction in [20, Lemma 3.3] shares the rank-2 incidence graph underlying the case k=1 of our construction. The higher-rank construction and its odd–even routing argument are independent and different.

Tool and computational resource disclosure.

GPT-5.6 Pro was used during exploratory brainstorming about possible constructions. The discussion was directed by formulating the required parameter scale and proposing higher rank spherical buildings as the geometric setting. The tool suggested splitting complete flags into their odd- and even-rank subflags, initially in connection with the edge problem. The authors developed this suggestion into the halved-flag construction, formulated and verified all mathematical arguments, and take full responsibility for the content. Generative-AI tools assisted in developing the accompanying Lean 4 formalization [10].
